facts.title: Named For Its Green Color
facts.text: Chlorine takes its name from the Greek word "chloros," meaning pale green or yellow-green, the exact color of the gas. At room temperature pure chlorine is a dense, choking yellow-green gas, which made it one of the few elements named directly for its appearance. The name was coined by Sir Humphry Davy in 1810.

facts.title: Davy Proved It An Element
facts.text: Carl Wilhelm Scheele first isolated the gas in 1774, but he believed it was a compound containing oxygen. It was Humphry Davy who, in 1810, demonstrated that the substance was a brand-new chemical element that could not be broken down further. His careful experiments overturned the prevailing chemistry of the time.

facts.title: The First Chemical Weapon
facts.text: On 22 April 1915 at Ypres, Belgium, German forces released around 168 tons of chlorine gas from cylinders, marking the first large-scale use of a chemical weapon in war. Because chlorine is denser than air, it sank into the trenches and forced soldiers out into the open. The horror of that day directly shaped the later Geneva Protocol banning chemical warfare.

facts.title: It Helped Defeat Cholera
facts.text: Adding tiny amounts of chlorine to drinking water kills bacteria, viruses, and parasites, and the practice dramatically reduced deadly diseases like cholera and typhoid in the early 1900s. Jersey City, New Jersey, became one of the first U.S. cities to continuously chlorinate its public water supply in 1908. Water chlorination is considered one of the most important public-health advances in history.

facts.title: You Are Eating It Daily
facts.text: Common table salt is sodium chloride, so every grain you sprinkle is roughly 60 percent chlorine by mass, locked safely as the chloride ion. In this form chlorine is not a poison gas at all but an essential nutrient. Chloride ions help your stomach make hydrochloric acid for digestion and keep the body's fluids in proper balance.

facts.title: Hidden Inside Most Plastics
facts.text: The "vinyl" in PVC stands for polyvinyl chloride, a tough plastic built around chlorine atoms that makes up pipes, window frames, flooring, and medical tubing. PVC is one of the world's most-produced plastics, and chlorine chemistry is essential to manufacturing it. Roughly a third of all chlorine produced industrially ends up in plastics like PVC.

facts.title: A Gas Made From Salt
facts.text: Industry produces chlorine by passing electricity through salty water (brine) in a process called the chlor-alkali process, splitting it into chlorine gas, hydrogen, and sodium hydroxide. This single reaction supplies almost all the chlorine humanity uses. It is one of the largest-scale electrochemical processes on Earth, consuming enormous amounts of electricity worldwide.

facts.title: Two Twins In Every Sample
facts.text: Natural chlorine is a mix of two stable isotopes, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37, in a roughly 3-to-1 ratio. Averaging them gives chlorine its distinctive atomic weight of about 35.45, one of the few that sits far from a whole number. Mass spectrometers see this 3:1 "chlorine pattern" as a tell-tale fingerprint when identifying molecules that contain it.

facts.title: A Thirsty Electron Grabber
facts.text: With seven electrons in its outer shell, chlorine is desperate to gain just one more to complete its set, making it fiercely reactive. This hunger gives it one of the highest electron affinities of any element and explains why it readily attacks metals and other substances. It is this reactivity that makes chlorine such a powerful disinfectant and bleaching agent.

facts.title: It Punched The Ozone Hole
facts.text: When chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) drift into the stratosphere, ultraviolet light frees their chlorine atoms, and a single chlorine atom can destroy tens of thousands of ozone molecules in a chain reaction. This discovery, honored with the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, revealed how CFCs were thinning Earth's protective ozone layer. The 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out CFCs, and the ozone layer is now slowly healing.
